summary: Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array.
mainInsight: Duplicates are detected by remembering what you have already seen: membership in a hash set is O(1), so one pass replaces comparing all pairs or sorting.

approaches.name: Sort then compare neighbours
approaches.summary: After sorting, equal values are adjacent; check nums[i] == nums[i+1].
approaches.interviewRelevance: Good answer when memory is constrained.

approaches.name: Hash set (one pass)
approaches.summary: Return true as soon as a value is already in the set; otherwise add it.

personalSolution.approach: Hash set (via dict) with early return
personalSolution.notes: A set would be more idiomatic; your comments also note the sort-based O(n log n)/O(1) alternative.

promptVariants: Which technique detects duplicates in O(n) time?
What data structure should 'have I seen this before?' suggest?
cards.explanation: A set answers membership in O(1) average, so a single pass finds the first repeat.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Two pointers: Two pointers needs sorted order; duplicates are not at symmetric positions.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Binary search: It needs sorted data and still O(n log n) overall with the sort.

promptVariants: Why is a set enough to solve Contains Duplicate?
cards.answer: We only need to know whether the current value was seen earlier, not where or how often. A hash set stores seen values with O(1) lookup, so one pass with early return suffices.
keyPoints: Return early on the first repeat
cards.explanation: Counts or indices (a dict) are unnecessary extra information.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the hash-set solution: ___
Contains Duplicate with a set runs in ___ time.
cards.explanation: Each element does one O(1) average lookup + insert.

promptVariants: What is the time-space trade-off between sorting and the hash-set approach?
Compare sort-based and set-based Contains Duplicate.
cards.answer: Set: O(n) time, O(n) extra space. Sort: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space if sorted in place (but it mutates the input). Choose the set unless memory is the constraint.

promptVariants: Your solution stores `counter[num] = 1` in a dict but never reads the value. What simpler structure expresses the same idea, and why is the return inside the loop correct?
Why can the loop return True the moment it sees a repeat, and what is a cleaner structure than a dict with dummy values?
cards.answer: A set: `if num in seen: return True; seen.add(num)`. The first time a value is already present we have proved a duplicate exists, so returning immediately is correct; reaching the end means every value was unique.
keyPoints: Use a set; the dict value is unused
Early return is safe: one repeat is enough

cards.explanation: A single element cannot repeat. The others each contain a repeated value.
